items.title: Avoiding Informal Conversations
items.quote: 1. Avoiding Informal Conversations: 👉 Those casual conversation at work are gold. They help you with exposure to everyday English usage, support the development of natural conversational skills and help you get noticed at work. ✅ So, instead of waiting for others to ask you questions, take the lead., Introduce yourself, open up and try to make “small talk”.

items.title: Overemphasis on Technical Jargon
items.quote: 2. Overemphasis on Technical Jargon: 👉I get it, technical words feel comfortable. You know them and you use them every day. But if you get a blank face or an embarrassed silence? In multicultural settings not everyone may be familiar with complex technical terms. ✅Find the right balance between technical jargon and plain language, and make sure your communication is clear.

items.title: Not Participating in Meetings
items.quote: 3. Not Participating in Meetings: 👉Instead of dreading the next team meeting, take control. Prepare some questions, reflect on your contribution and talk about what you do. ✅This is the best way to build confidence and overcome that fear of making mistakes.

items.title: Lack of Proactive Learning
items.quote: 4. Lack of Proactive Learning: 👉Company courses are good, and they are usually free. But what if they never come? Or if they are too late? Waiting for formal language training can actually slow you down. ✅Take ownership of your language skills and start improving them independently. Be proactive.

items.title: Fear of Feedback
items.quote: 5. Fear of Feedback: 👉Feedback is a powerful tool for growth. Let’s use it effectively to boost our confidence. How? ↳ Be specific. ↳ Choose the right person. ↳ Set a positive tone. ✅Once you get some feedback, create a practical action plan. For instance, if pronunciation is highlighted, practice those specific sounds regularly. Remember, confidence is a skill, and it can be developed and improved. You have more control over it than you think. Am I missing anything? Let me know in the comments.

items.quote: ⭕ Satisfied vs. Satisfying: Example: "The customer was satisfied with our service." (personal feeling) Example: "Providing excellent customer service is satisfying for our team." (causing satisfaction)

items.quote: ⭕ Bored vs. Boring: Example: "I was bored in the meeting without relevant discussions." (personal feeling) Example: "Repetitive tasks can be boring for employees." (causing boredom)

items.title: Surprised vs. Surprising
items.quote: ⭕ Surprised vs. Surprising: Example: "I was surprised by the unexpected announcement." (personal feeling) Example: "The sudden increase in sales was surprising." (causing surprise)

items.title: Motivated vs. Motivating
items.quote: ⭕ Motivated vs. Motivating: Example: "I'm motivated to achieve my career goals." (personal feeling) Example: "Recognition can be motivating for employees." (causing motivation)

items.title: Focused vs. Focusing

items.quote: 3. Find a mentor. ➜ Seek guidance and support as well as valuable feedback. Learn from the best. 👉 “I've been really impressed by your expertise. Would you be open to sharing your insights and guidance with me as I navigate my career path in IT?”

items.title: Build a network
items.quote: 4. Build a network. ➜ Be open with your peers, colleagues and management. Join virtual (social network) and real networks. Make the most of company events and use “small talk”. 👉 "Hi there! How are you finding the event so far? I noticed your name badge - are you part of the Finance department? Have you been to similar events before?"

items.title: Be active in team meetings
items.quote: 5. Be active in team meetings. ➜ Ask questions, volunteer to present part of the agenda, offer to take notes, contribute with well-thought questions. 👉 “I've been thinking about our current project, and I believe we could improve the UX integrating the new layout. What are your thoughts on this?"

items.title: Make the most of your 1 to 1’s
items.quote: 6. Make the most of your 1 to 1’s ➜ Listen to and use the feedback you receive. Make sure you share your expectations and growth plan with your leader. If you keep silent, they won’t know. 👉 “Could we schedule some time to discuss potential opportunities for development and how I can best align my goals with the team's objectives?"

items.title: Make your work visible
items.quote: 7. Make your work visible. ➜ It’s not only about doing the work. But also making sure people know. Talk & write about it. Ask for 5 minutes in your next team meeting, write a newsletter, email your leader asking for advice. 👉 "I wanted to share an update on the project that I've been working on. The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: Unemployed
items.quote: 1. Unemployed Definition: Not having a job. Example: "After the company downsized, several IT professionals found themselves unemployed and started looking for new opportunities."

items.title: Self-Employed
items.quote: 2. Self-Employed Definition: Working for oneself as a freelancer or the owner of a business rather than for an employer. Example: "After years in corporate IT, Sarah decided to become self-employed and started her own cybersecurity consulting firm."

items.title: Part-Time
items.quote: 3. Part-Time Definition: Working fewer hours than a full-time job, often less than 35 hours a week. Example: "To balance his studies and work, John took a part-time position as a junior developer at a tech startup."

items.title: Temporary
items.quote: 4. Temporary Definition: Working for a limited period. Example: "During the project implementation phase, we hired a temporary IT specialist to help manage the increased workload."

items.title: Work For
items.quote: 5. Work For Definition: To be employed by someone or an organization. Example: "I work for a leading software development company, focusing on project management and team coordination."

items.title: To Be in Charge of
items.quote: 6. To Be in Charge of Definition: To have control or responsibility for something. Example: "As the IT manager, I am in charge of overseeing the network infrastructure and ensuring system security."

items.title: To Be Responsible For
items.quote: 7. To Be Responsible For Definition: To have a duty to take care of something or someone. Example: "I am responsible for the performance and development of my team, making sure they meet our project deadlines."

items.title: To Be Sacked (or Fired)
items.quote: 8. To Be Sacked (or Fired) Definition: To be dismissed from a job. Example: "Unfortunately, due to repeated security breaches, the IT director was sacked for failing to protect company data."

items.title: Set Up a Company
items.quote: 9. Set Up a Company Definition: To start a new business. items.title: Effective Communication
items.quote: 1. 𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 ↳If you have an ‘ok’ level, can you explain complex technical issues to non-technical stakeholders? ↳Skill: Active listening and clear articulation to ensure that your team understands expectations and goals.

items.title: Emotional Intelligence (EQ)
items.quote: 2. 𝗘𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝗘𝗤) ↳Empathy, persuasion, conflict resolution. In English! Tone, politeness, and cultural nuances can be tricky. ↳Skill: Fluency in English to better express understanding, manage emotions, and resolve conflicts to lead teams more effectively.

items.title: Leadership & Teamwork
items.quote: 3. 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 & 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗺𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 ↳Can you motivate others in English? Do you know how to be assertive? ↳Skill: English proficiency in specific contexts (e.g., giving feedback, negotiation) to help develop leadership and collaborative abilities.

items.title: Cultural Sensitivity
items.quote: 4. 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 ↳You need to adapt your language to the multicultural context. (Yeas, jokes and humour too). ↳Skill: Improving English skills helps you navigate these cultural nuances, building stronger relationships with international colleagues and clients.

items.title: Presentation and Public Speaking
items.quote: 5. 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 ↳You have the technical knowledge but struggle with presenting your ideas to management or clients (again, in English!). This can limit your career progression. ↳Skill: Improving your English presentation skills enables you to communicate confidently in meetings and pitch ideas.

items.title: Problem-Solving and Critical Thinking
items.quote: 6. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺-𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 ↳You often need to discuss problems, brainstorm solutions, and work through complex issues. This needs precise language skills to avoid misunderstandings. ↳Skill: Proficiency in English allows you to better express logical reasoning and propose solutions in a way that is understandable to all.

items.title: Networking and Professional Relationships
items.quote: 7. 𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 ↳Networking often means that you need to talk to people. Chats, emails are not enough. You might find yourself limited if you aren’t comfortable with informal conversation in English. ↳Skill: Small talk! This will help you be more confident in networking situations, contributing to better professional relationships and opportunities. This is an ongoing journey. It needs training and dedication. Focus on English for work scenarios, for giving feedback

items.title: Focus on your strengths.
items.quote: 1. Focus on your strengths. ➜ Reflect on what makes you unique (not what the others expect of you). Use your style. At the beginning, prioritize quality over quantity (and speed). 👉 "I believe in taking the time to ensure accuracy and precision in my work, which ultimately leads to better outcomes."

items.title: Refine your language.
items.quote: 2. Refine your language. ➜ Learn how to be effective but professional at the same time. Be patient. 👉 “FIRST we’ll discuss the upgrade, THEN we’ll submit it for approval, FINALLY, we’ll implement it” “Could you 𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 help me with my report?”

items.title: Find a mentor.
items.quote: 3. Find a mentor. ➜ Seek guidance, support and valuable feedback. Learn from the best. 👉 “I'm really impressed by your expertise. Could I ask you a few questions to clarify this process ands maybe get a few extra ideas on my personal development?”

items.title: Build a network.
items.quote: 4. Build a network. ➜ Be open with your peers, colleagues and management. Join virtual (social network) and real networks. Make the most of company events and use “small talk”. 👉 "Hi there! How are you finding the event so far? I noticed your name badge - are you part of the Finance department? Have you been to similar events before?"

items.title: Be active in team meetings.
items.quote: 5. Be active in team meetings. ➜ Ask questions, volunteer to present part of the agenda, offer to take notes, contribute with well-thought questions. 👉 “I've been thinking about our current project, and I believe we could improve the UX integrating the new layout. What are your thoughts on this?"

items.title: Make the most of your 1 to 1’s
items.quote: 6. Make the most of your 1 to 1’s ➜ Listen to and use the feedback you receive. Make sure you share your expectations and growth plan with your leader. If you keep silent, they won’t know. 👉 “Could we schedule some time to discuss potential opportunities for development and how I can best align my goals with the team's objectives?"

items.title: Make your work visible.
items.quote: 7. Make your work visible. ➜ It’s not only about doing the work. But also making sure people know. Talk & write about it. Ask for 5 minutes in your next team meeting, write a newsletter, email your leader asking for advice. 👉 "I wanted to share an update on the project that I've been working on. The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: Take care of yourself.
items.quote: 8. Take care of yourself. ➜ Stay active both mentally and physically. Mind your own wellbeing so it reflects at work. 👉 “I've been implementing deep breathing and short breaks to help manage stress levels during busy periods, and I've found it really beneficial." items.title: Grammar: Sound Professional without Overthinking Every Sentence

items.title: Speaking English isn’t the same as connecting globally
items.quote: Speaking English isn’t the same as connecting globally. English may be the common language in international business… But it’s not always a shared one. You can have the right words. The right grammar. The right tone (in your culture, at least)… …and still miss the mark entirely. Why? Because language is not enough We need to be aware of 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁. items.quote: Here’s a nerdy (but true) reason the summer slide happens… Have you ever heard of Ebbinghaus’ Forgetting Curve? You can hack the curve! ✅ Repetition over time ✅ Re‑exposure to the same material Every time you review or practice something, the curve flattens, and your knowledge sticks around longer. items.title: Focus on your strengths.
items.quote: 𝟭. 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝘀. ➜ Reflect on what makes you unique (not what the others expect of you). Use your style. At the beginning, prioritize quality over quantity (and speed). 👉 "I believe in taking the time to ensure accuracy and precision in my work, which ultimately leads to better outcomes."

items.title: Refine your language.
items.quote: 𝟮. 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲. ➜ Learn how to be effective but professional at the same time. Be patient. 👉 “FIRST we’ll discuss the upgrade, THEN we’ll submit it for approval, FINALLY, we’ll implement it” “Could you 𝗽𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 help me with my report?”

items.title: Find a mentor.
items.quote: 𝟯. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿. ➜ Seek guidance, support and valuable feedback. Learn from the best. 👉 “I'm really impressed by your expertise. Could I ask you a few questions to clarify this process ands maybe get a few extra ideas on my personal development?”

items.title: Build a network.
items.quote: 𝟰. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸. ➜ Be open with your peers, colleagues and management. Join virtual (social network) and real networks. Make the most of company events and use “small talk”. 👉 "Hi there! How are you finding the event so far? I noticed your name badge - are you part of the Finance department? Have you been to similar events before?"

items.title: Be active in team meetings.
items.quote: 𝟱. 𝗕𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀. ➜ Ask questions, volunteer to present part of the agenda, offer to take notes, contribute with well-thought questions. 👉 “I've been thinking about our current project, and I believe we could improve the UX integrating the new layout. What are your thoughts on this?"

items.title: Make the most of 1 to 1's.
items.quote: 𝟲. 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝟭 𝘁𝗼 𝟭’𝘀 ➜ Listen to and use the feedback you receive. Make sure you share your expectations and growth plan with your leader. If you keep silent, they won’t know. 👉 “Could we schedule some time to discuss potential opportunities for development and how I can best align my goals with the team's objectives?"

items.title: Make your work visible.
items.quote: 𝟳. 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲. ➜ It’s not only about doing the work. But also making sure people know. Talk & write about it. Ask for 5 minutes in your next team meeting, write a newsletter, email your leader asking for advice. 👉 "I wanted to share an update on the project that I've been working on. The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: Take care of yourself.
items.quote: 𝟴. 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳. ➜ Stay active both mentally and physically. Mind your own wellbeing so it reflects at work. 👉 “I've been implementing deep breathing and short breaks to help manage stress levels during busy periods, and I've found it really beneficial." items.quote: 1️⃣ 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 You give context. Then more context. Then background to the background. What it signals: “I’m not sure this will stand on its own.” In leadership-level communication, clarity beats completeness. State the decision first. Explain after (if needed).

items.title: Softening decisions
items.quote: 2️⃣ 𝗦𝗼𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 “I think maybe we could consider…” “Perhaps one option might be…” What it signals: “This isn’t firm.” Senior stakeholders don’t expect certainty about the future. They expect 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆, not fluency. Clear recommendation. Clear reasoning. That’s authority.

items.title: Apologizing before speaking

items.title: Why Team Communication Breaks Down
items.quote: Why Team Communication Breaks Down Most team issues aren’t technical. They’re communication problems.

items.title: Word Stress
items.quote: 1️⃣ 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀: 𝗘𝗺𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝘀 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 In technical discussions, stress determines what people remember. Compare: “I think we could consider changing the architecture…” vs “I recommend changing the 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.” The emphasis directs attention. Attention shapes authority. 📌 Focus on stressing the words that carry decisions, risk, or impact — not filler phrases.

items.title: Intonation
items.quote: 2️⃣ 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝗧𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗖𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘆 Your voice pattern signals intention. Rising tone ↗️ can sound tentative. Flat tone ➖ can sound disengaged. Falling tone ↘️ signals completion and certainty. In leadership communication, controlled falling intonation often communicates clarity and decision. 📌 Practice finishing recommendations with a downward tone. It subtly increases perceived confidence.

items.title: Connected Speech
items.quote: 3️⃣ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗰𝗵: 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗙𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 When speech flows naturally, listeners focus on meaning instead of form. If delivery is too segmented, your audience works harder to follow you — and cognitive load shifts to them. Smoother linking improves: clarity in fast exchanges listening comprehension executive presence 📌 Record short work-related sentences. Notice where your speech becomes rigid or over-controlled.

Here’s what that shift looks like in practice when you HACK your English 👇 🅗 𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗲: 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 You stop learning generic English. You practise how you actually work: • explaining technical deci

items.quote: You don’t build an international career by waiting until your English is “ready.” Sometimes… you just get dropped into Japan. No plan. Limited English. No way back. And suddenly… you have no choice but to speak. In Episode 36 of The Non-Native Leader - Podcast, Mario Crea (Head of Digital Transformation Philip Morris International) shares exactly this. He didn’t start with perfect English. He found himself in an international environment in Japan surrounded by people speaking different languages

items.title: Fillers take over
items.quote: 𝟭. 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 “Uhm… ehm… aaaah…” 👉 Why: you’re buying time 👉 Fix: Replace fillers with pause. Literally stop. Silence sounds confident.

items.title: You apologize before speaking
items.quote: 𝟮. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 “Sorry for my English…” “Maybe this is wrong, but…” 👉 Why: lowering expectations 👉 Fix: start with the message ❌ “Sorry, maybe I’m wrong but…” ✅ “From what I see, the issue is…”

items.title: You soften everything
items.quote: 𝟯. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 “Maybe… perhaps… I think…” 👉 Why: avoiding sounding too strong 👉 Fix: be direct, then support your point ❌ “I’m not sure but maybe we could consider…” ✅ “One option is to…”

items.title: You rush to the end
items.quote: 𝟰. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱 Words blur. Clarity drops. 👉 Why: you want to get it over with 👉 Fix: slow down on purpose Clarity > speed

items.title: You restart mid-sentence
items.quote: 𝟱. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝗱-𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 “So basically… no wait… actually…” 👉 Why: building while speaking 👉 Fix: use simple structures → “The issue is…” → “What I suggest is…”

items.title: You over-explain
items.quote: 𝟲. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻 Too many details. No clear direction. 👉 Why: translating your thinking 👉 Fix: say less, structure more → Point → Explanation → Impact Here’s the shift most people miss: Confidence doesn’t come from better English. It comes from removing hesitation signals. items.title: Start with direction
items.quote: 1️⃣ 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Don't make people guess where you're going. ❌ Instead of: "I was just thinking that maybe we could..." ✅ Try: "My recommendation is..." or "The point I'd like to raise is..." The first sentence should reduce uncertainty, not create it.

items.title: Lead with the point
items.quote: 2️⃣ 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 Many professionals explain everything... before saying what they actually mean. History. Background. Exceptions. Technical details. By the time they reach the point... the room has already moved on. A much better structure is: Point → Reason → Detail For example: "I recommend delaying the release by one week. The main reason is quality risk. We still have two unresolved issues in the payment flow." Simple. Logical. Easy to follow.

items.title: Structure beats certainty
items.quote: 3️⃣ 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘆 You don't need to sound 100% certain. You do need to sound organised. ❌ "Maybe... I'm not sure... perhaps..." ✅ "I see two possible options." or "My initial view is..." People don't expect you to know everything. They do expect you to think clearly.

items.title: Finish with a recommendation
items.quote: 4️⃣ 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Senior communication doesn't stop at information. It ends with direction. Instead of finishing with: "So... that's the situation." Finish with: ✅ "My recommendation is..." ✅ "The next step is..." ✅ "What I'd suggest is..." Never leave people wondering: "So... what do we do now?"

items.title: Replace filler words with pauses
items.quote: 5️⃣ 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲𝘀 When your brain needs a second... don't fill the silence. ❌ "Uhm..." "Basically..." "You know..." "How can I say..." Pause. Think. Continue. A short pause sounds far more confident than a sentence full of filler words.
